title: Lakshmi Chooses
hookLine: Lakshmi rises from the churned ocean holding a garland, and looks over every suitor before she chooses
carry: lakshmi chooses, and stays beside vishnu
tomorrow: before she held a veena, saraswati was a river

lines: GODS AND DEMONS CHURN THE OCEAN.
cards: The worlds are dim, and the gods are losing.

So they make a truce with their enemies, and together gods and demons churn the ocean of milk, a mountain for the churning stick and a great serpent for the rope, pulling back and forth like a cosmic tug of war.
Strange things come up out of the foam. Then, standing on a lotus, holding a lotus, radiant, the goddess herself rises from the waves. Every god and every demon on that shore wants her.
Today Lakshmi comes back, and gets to choose.

teach.h: THE OCEAN GIVES HER A GARLAND.
teach.b: In the Vishnu Purana the moment is pure celebration.
The rivers come to bathe her, the ocean gives her a garland of unfading flowers, the gods sing her praises, and she goes straight to Vishnu and rests on his chest, and the worlds brighten again.
But the Bhagavata Purana slows the moment down and gives Lakshmi a long look. Garland in hand, she walks along the line of suitors, studying them, and finds something missing in each.
One has great austerity but hasn't conquered anger.
One has knowledge but can't let go of attachment. One is mighty but can't master desire. One is generous, another devoted to duty, and still each falls short somewhere.
Then she comes to Vishnu, the one who isn't reaching for her at all, and places the garland on him. That's the character in one scene.
Lakshmi isn't a prize handed to the winner; nobody wins her by pulling hardest on the rope. She looks, she weighs, she chooses.
Having chosen, tradition says, she stays at his side and goes with him when he comes into the world: some tell of her as Sita beside Rama, and as Rukmini beside Krishna.

That's why, in so many temples and homes, Lakshmi and Vishnu are worshipped together as Lakshmi-Narayana, and why she's pictured resting on his chest: fortune that chose to stay beside the one who preserves the world.
Yesterday she left where she wasn't honored.

teach.h: SHE LOOKS, SHE WEIGHS, SHE CHOOSES.
teach.b: Today she chooses where she'll stay. Lakshmi isn't luck that just happens. She chooses.

how: Lakshmi is shown seated or standing on a lotus, often beside Vishnu, and Hindus honor her at home and in temples, especially on the night of Lakshmi puja at Diwali.

games.q: you're Lakshmi, rising from the ocean with a garland in your hands. every god and demon on the shore wants you. what do you do?
o: walk the line, study each one, then choose
drop it and go back into the sea
games.why: in the Bhagavata Purana she studies each suitor, finds something missing in each, and places the garland on Vishnu.

practice: Bring to mind one choice in front of you, small or large, and don't decide yet: look down the line the way Lakshmi did, one option at a time, noticing what each is missing, without grabbing the loudest.
Then let it rest; some choices come clear only after a long look. If you pray, ask for good judgment in your own words; if you don't, just keep looking.

wordCard.voice: Durga. The name this run of five goddesses sits under; today it belongs to Lakshmi, rising from the ocean, garland in hand. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune and prosperity, also called Shri; she rises from the churned ocean on a lotus.
